text:
The water found the bookcase first, in the way water always finds things, without announcement and without malice, which is how Dr. Ruth Amsel would later describe it, and she would have liked to add that water is also the most democratic element in the building, since it has never once been known to discriminate among the faculty.

It was April, the year the university celebrated its sesquicentennial with a commemorative fountain that ran on tap water and a brochure promising that "our facilities reflect our values." Dr. Amsel, who taught historical linguistics and had spent thirty years studying how people talk about things they cannot control, was in her office, a room the size of a decent closet, pulling books down for an article on the Indo-European roots of weather words. She got to the shelf of wax cylinders, the field recordings she had spent a decade collecting of a dialect spoken by fewer people than lived in her building, and felt the cardboard loosen in her hands. She pulled the bookcase from the wall and there it was: a tide-line, dark and even, running across the plaster at the height of her hip, and beneath it the slow beading of moisture coming up through the floor like a rumor.

The building was the old municipal waterworks annex on Ninth Street, built in 1962 for the Department of Water and Power, a fact the university had found useful, since it meant the structure had been engineered with an abundance of concrete and a scarcity of imagination. The linguistics faculty had moved in when the university expanded, and with them a collection of endangered-language recordings housed in a storage room that facilities had once described, in writing, as "a dry room, nominally." Dr. Amsel had written the word *nominally* on an index card and filed it with the others, which was what Mrs. Blythe, the department secretary, had been doing for four decades: filing everything, complaints and compliments and requests for better coffee, into a manila box that grew heavier each year and was never, by anyone's account, destroyed.

When Dr. Amsel reported the water, the response was so practiced it had the texture of a reflex. Ms. Diane Farrow of facilities came with a clipboard and rubber boots and examined the wall with the expression of a doctor whose patient has already been written off in the chart. She said the annex had a "moisture situation," that a contractor had been scheduled, and that the work would be "disruptive but temporary," which are the two words that came to function in the building as a kind of weather forecast: it may rain, and the rain will be temporary.

The contractor came in May and drilled into the ceiling of the phonetics laboratory, where Dr. Ingrid Solberg kept her spectrograph. The dust that fell was the color of old flour and settled on the spectrograph's keys, on the graduate students' theses, on Dr. Solberg's own hands, which she washed that night until her knuckles ached, and which did not entirely clear the taste of plaster from her mouth. The contractor had come to inspect the roof deck. There was no membrane, he said, in a tone suggesting the absence of a membrane was something one could be surprised by, like finding no steering wheel in a car. The membrane was the critical waterproofing layer, the sheet of rubberized asphalt specified in the original plans of 1961 and never installed, because the contractor of 1962 had been paid on a schedule, and the schedule had ended.

The information moved through the faculty the way it always moved, chair to committee, committee to meeting, meeting to hallway, where it was spoken in the lowered voice people use for institutional news, as if volume might determine truth. Dr. Owen Pell, the department chair, told the faculty the university was "taking the matter very seriously" and that repairs would be "phased in order to minimize impact on instructional schedules." Dr. Amsel looked at her wax cylinders, wrapped in cloth in a room whose walls had begun to smell of wet stone, and thought about how the oldest weather words she knew had once also meant the season of planting, and how that connection had worn away somewhere, leaving only what happens to you whether you like it or not.

The first phase lasted from May through November. It consisted of the roof being torn off and replaced, then torn off again because the new contractor had laid the deck wrong, then the membrane being installed, then removed again because it had been sourced from a supplier that, in Ms. Farrow's phrase, "had some quality-control issues." During this period the faculty met in the basement of the First Congregational Church on Delancey, a room that smelled of pipe organ and floor wax, with no acoustics, no whiteboard, and no chairs for the graduate students, who sat on the pews with laptops in their laps and looked, by all accounts, like a congregation that had been interrupted.

The second phase was worse, because it was inside. To install drainage away from the foundation, the contractor had to dig into the archive room, which turned out to contain asbestos, and so the work stopped, then stopped again, then began again under different rules, in different suits, at different hours, which were the hours the university chose to schedule the noisiest drilling, ten to one, overlapping precisely with the only lecture slot Dr. Amsel had ever held. She kept it in the end by teaching from the stairwell, door open, voice raised against the jackhammer, and the graduate students, to her lasting credit and their lasting bewilderment, transcribed without complaint.

The health effects arrived on schedule, the way effects always do. Dr. Solberg's inhaler became a daily companion and then a twice-daily one, and eventually she taught her seminars from her car in the lot, a practice she defended as efficient. Two graduate students reported headaches that their doctors attributed, in the polite plural, to "the environment." The mold appeared in the east stairwell in October, a dark velvety thing that Ms. Farrow acknowledged with the word "colonization," and the faculty came to speak of the mold as having colonized them, the way they had been colonized by the schedule, the phases, the temporary that kept proving itself permanent.

There were moments of genuine peril. In February, during a hard rain, water came through the ceiling of the archive room in a thin, steady sheet, and the graduate student on duty, a young man named Tomás, who had recently learned enough of the dialect in question to transcribe its songs, spent the afternoon standing in the doorway with a trash can, catching it as best he could, while Dr. Amsel drove over from her house with a tarpaulin and a sense of the occasion she did not allow herself to feel too large. Nothing was lost. This is worth stating plainly, because it is the kind of fact a university loves and a story does not always have, and because it mattered to Dr. Amsel more than the loss would have. The cylinders dried. The tapes survived. The songs, sung by the last fluent speakers of a language that has no word for waterproofing, went on being sung, in a sense, inside the wax, waiting for ears.

What changed over the second winter was the faculty's relationship to the building itself. There is a stage in any long siege, institutional or otherwise, in which the besieged stop pretending it is temporary, and the linguistics faculty passed through it sometime in March, at a church-basement meeting, when Dr. Pell announced that the third phase, the proper membrane, the real one, from a supplier with no quality-control issues, was scheduled for the following spring, "pending final budget approval," and everyone in the room laughed, not cruelly, but with the relief of people who have found the one joke that fits.

They adapted, though adaptation, Dr. Amsel would say, was the one skill the building taught reliably, and she made the point in lectures, not meetings, where it might have sounded like criticism. The graduate students organized the archive's dusting as a rotation, wiping shelves with dry cloths, checking the humidity gauge, reporting the number to Mrs. Blythe, who wrote it on an index card. Meetings moved to seven in the evening, in the quiet, and the department found it had been having better discussions than in years, the kind of gift disruption sometimes gives, unbidden and unwelcome as a gift from an enemy. The church basement grew its own traditions: a jar for complaints nobody ever paid out of, a chalkboard for the day's drilling schedule, a standing joke that the pipe organ was the only thing in the room properly waterproofed since 1962.

The third phase came the following spring, and this time the contractor stayed. The membrane was laid in a single weather window, a week of clear days, with no quality-control issues. The roof was sealed, the drainage connected, and in June the building was given back with a ribbon that Ms. Farrow cut with the air of a woman closing a wound she had been dressing for three years.

Dr. Amsel moved her office back in July and stood in the dry room with the bookcase against the wall and the tide-line gone, sanded out, painted over, and waited, with the patience of a woman who had spent three years learning to wait, for the first hard rain. It came on a Tuesday in September, a proper autumn storm, the kind that used to mean nothing to her at all. She went upstairs and put her ear to the ceiling and heard the rain come down on the new roof, a sound like the building breathing evenly for the first time in years, and she thought about how the faculty would take this in, which is to say they would notice it, and thank Ms. Farrow, and move on to the next complaint, because that is what they are, a faculty, and complaints are their native tongue.

At the September meeting, Dr. Pell announced that the university had approved a fourth phase, "at a future date," for the archive room: proper climate control, sealed shelving, a humidity system that would keep the recordings safe without the daily vigil of a young man and a trash can. He used the phrase "pending final budget approval," and the room laughed again, and then settled, because beneath the joke there was something else now, something the three years had deposited in them like sediment, a willingness to believe a schedule when it arrived, even a future one, even a pending one.

Mrs. Blythe started a new box of index cards that September. On the first card she wrote, in her careful hand: *Archive climate control, approved in principle. Phase four. Spring, hopefully.*

Dr. Amsel read it over her shoulder and said, "Hopefully is doing a lot of work in that sentence."

"I know," Mrs. Blythe said. "I've always said that about weather."

Outside, the rain continued, and the building held it off, and inside the annex, in offices that smelled of dry plaster and old paper, the faculty went back to work, resigned to the pace of institutions, enduring as people endure, which is to say one phase at a time, and hoping, without quite committing to the word, for spring.
